title: The three hours
hook: some churches keep noon to three on Good Friday with his seven last words

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyrenian: a walk with stops, and Simon carrying the beam behind Jesus. Your line was step by step with him. What did you take one stop at a time? Day one thousand thirty-two.

"Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." That's Matthew, in the King James Bible, describing the afternoon of the crucifixion. The sixth hour to the ninth: on our clocks, around noon to three. On Good Friday, some churches keep exactly those hours. The doors stay open. People come in on a lunch break and leave again, or sit through the whole afternoon. There are readings, a few hymns, and long stretches of silence. And running through it, one at a time, are the things Jesus said from the cross. Today, the three hours.

Start with the texts themselves. No single Gospel has all of them. Tradition gathers seven sayings from the four Gospels and sets them in an order. In Luke, Jesus says, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." To a criminal crucified beside him, who asks to be remembered, he says, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." In John, he looks down at his mother and his friend: "Woman, behold thy son!" and to the friend, "Behold thy mother!" Then the cry Matthew and Mark both keep: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" the first line of Psalm 22. Back in John: "I thirst." Then: "It is finished." And Luke's last: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Now look at the shape the order makes. The first three words are for other people: the ones killing him, a stranger dying next to him, his mother. In that much pain, he's still giving things away. Then the dark center, the cry of being forsaken, prayed in the words of a psalm. Then the body: thirst. Then the work done. Then trust. Christians hear different things in the sayings, and the churches that keep the three hours may preach on each in turn. But the order alone teaches something. It moves from others, through abandonment, to rest in God's hands. The three hours give each word room, so none of them gets rushed.

Here's the practice: read the seven words. Slowly, with one breath between each, aloud or under your breath. Forgive them, for they know not what they do. Today, paradise. Behold thy son. Behold thy mother. Why hast thou forsaken me. I thirst. It is finished. Into thy hands. Then go back to whichever one caught on something, and stay with it for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can let it become your prayer. If you don't, just let it sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Good Friday, the day Christians keep noon to three with silence, readings, and the seven words from the cross.
Your line: the seven words. Today, choose one of the seven and carry it with you until three o'clock this afternoon, or tomorrow's if three has passed. Day one thousand thirty-two.

howItsDone: Some churches hold a Good Friday service from noon to three, with readings, hymns, silence and short meditations on each of the seven sayings of Jesus from the cross; people may stay for part or all of it.

notes: Claims rule: 'seven' is the tradition's count, and each saying is cited; the split (Luke three, John three, Matthew and Mark one shared) is counted from the cited texts. The outline's 'many churches' is softened to 'some churches'; no history of the devotion is given.
'On our clocks, around noon to three' converts the sixth and ninth hours; confirm phrasing.
Mark 15:34 KJV renders the cry 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' identically to Matthew 27:46; confirm.
